home: Sirius for Sustainable Resilience (SSR) Empowering Youth for Lasting Change A women-led civil society organization in Tigray & Addis Ababa, empowering youth, women, and marginalized communities through peace, rights, and digital inclusion. Choose a path below:
about: About Sirius for Sustainable Resilience (SSR) SSR is a non-profit, non-political, women-led CSO founded in Tigray, Ethiopia. We empower marginalized communities, youth, and women through capacity building, advocacy, and opportunity creation. Mission To empower youth and marginalized groups through capacity building, advocacy, and meaningful participation in creating a safe and peaceful environment. Vision An inclusive and enabling environment with an empowered society achieving sustainable development. Our thematic areas • Empowerment of marginalized communities • Youth and women empowerment • Peacebuilding and social cohesion • Human rights advocacy • Economic resilience and digital inclusion Who we serve Youth and women • Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) • Marginalized and conflict-affected communities Our values Sustainability • Service • Resilience

gbv.menu: Gender-Based Violence (GBV) Clear, respectful information to help you understand GBV, know your rights, stay safer, and find support. This bot shares information only. It is not a crisis counseling service. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, contact local emergency services or a trusted support provider. Choose a guide:
gbv.what: What is Gender-Based Violence? GBV is harm directed at a person because of their gender. It can include physical, sexual, emotional, economic, or online abuse. Important truths • GBV is never the survivor's fault • It can happen in homes, schools, workplaces, or communities • Anyone can be affected — women and girls face higher risk • Silence protects abuse; support and accountability protect people Understanding GBV is a first step toward safer communities.
gbv.rights: Your rights matter Every person has the right to safety, dignity, and bodily autonomy. You have the right to: • Live free from violence and intimidation • Seek help without shame or blame • Be heard with respect and confidentiality • Access information, healthcare, and justice support • Make decisions about your own recovery and next steps Knowing your rights helps you advocate for yourself and others.
gbv.safety: Practical safety ideas • Tell a trusted person where you are when you feel unsafe • Keep emergency contacts easy to reach • If possible, move to a safer public space when threatened • Document incidents only if it is safe to do so • Online: protect passwords, avoid sharing location publicly, and block/report harassment Safety plans look different for everyone. Choose what fits your situation — your judgment matters.
gbv.support: If someone confides in you • Listen without judgment • Believe them — do not ask what they "did wrong" • Respect privacy; do not share their story without consent • Ask how you can help, rather than taking over • Encourage professional or community support when needed Supportive communities reduce stigma and help survivors heal.
gbv.help: Get help & resources If you need support, you are not alone. SSR contact Zemen Desta, Executive Director Phone: +251 939 367 178 Email: zemufani@gmail.com Locations: Mekelle, Tigray & Addis Ababa Please remember This bot provides digital information. For urgent danger, contact local emergency services, police, a health facility, or a trusted protection actor in your area. SSR works to create safer spaces for youth and women — reach out if you want guidance on community programs.

peace.menu: Peacebuilding & Social Cohesion SSR strengthens trust, dialogue, and peaceful coexistence within and between communities — especially among youth. Explore a short guide:
peace.why: Why peacebuilding matters Conflict damages trust, education, livelihoods, and hope. Peacebuilding helps communities rebuild relationships and prevent cycles of harm. Inclusive peace means youth, women, and marginalized groups have a real voice in decisions that shape their future.
peace.dialogue: Dialogue & peaceful coexistence Practical ways to contribute: • Listen across differences before reacting • Challenge rumors with verified information • Create spaces where people feel safe to speak • Support local initiatives that bring communities together Small acts of respect and dialogue build social cohesion over time.
peace.youth: Youth role in peace Young people are not only affected by conflict — they are agents of lasting change. SSR invests in youth leadership, skills, and participation so "Sirius" young people can drive inclusive and peaceful solutions in their communities.
peace.rumors: Rumors and trust False rumors can restart fear and conflict. • Pause before sharing unverified claims • Ask where information came from • Encourage community dialogue instead of blame • Support local fact-checkers and peace actors Trust grows when people feel heard and informed.
peace.skills: Peace skills for youth Practical skills SSR promotes: • Active listening • Mediation basics • Inclusive facilitation • Non-violent communication • Planning community dialogue sessions These skills help youth lead peaceful change in schools, IDP sites, and neighborhoods.

rights.menu: Human Rights Advocacy SSR promotes awareness, protection, and advocacy for fundamental human rights — with a focus on women and youth. Choose a guide:
rights.basics: Human rights basics Human rights are freedoms and protections every person has simply because they are human — including dignity, equality, safety, education, and participation. Rights are universal: they apply to everyone, everywhere, without discrimination.
rights.women_youth: Women & youth focus Women and youth often face barriers to safety, voice, and opportunity — especially after conflict or displacement. SSR centers their leadership and participation so advocacy reflects real community needs, not top-down decisions alone.
rights.engage: How you can engage • Learn and share accurate rights information • Stand with people whose rights are denied • Join peaceful community and CSO initiatives • Contact SSR to learn about programs and partnerships Advocacy starts with awareness — and grows through collective action.
rights.advocacy_steps: Advocacy steps 1. Learn the issue and the rights involved 2. Document facts safely and accurately 3. Build allies (youth, women, CSOs) 4. Choose peaceful channels (meetings, petitions, media) 5. Follow up and protect people at risk Advocacy is strongest when communities lead and stay safe.
rights.duty_bearers: Duty-bearers and accountability Duty-bearers (government offices, institutions, service providers) have obligations to respect, protect, and fulfill rights. Communities can: • Ask clear questions about services • Use complaint and referral pathways • Partner with CSOs like SSR for accompaniment • Demand inclusion of women and youth in decisions
